Toxicology Chapter 181

Lithium

Lithium toxicity is a renal-sodium-volume problem with neurologic consequences. Serum levels help, but clinical severity depends heavily on acute vs chronic exposure, renal function, sodium/volume status, and CNS burden.

Board lens: chronic toxicity = neurologic symptoms at levels that may not look dramatic. Sustained-release ingestion = delayed absorption. Activated charcoal does not bind lithium.

Overview and Pharmacology

Tintinalli Source Check
AcuteGI symptoms first; serum may rise before CNS distribution.
ChronicNeurologic symptoms predominate because brain/tissue burden is higher.
Acute-on-chronicWorst of both worlds: existing tissue burden plus new ingestion.

Pharmacokinetics

Tintinalli Source Check
Must remember: lithium is handled like sodium by the kidney. Dehydration, sodium depletion, NSAIDs, thiazides/loops, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, low-output states, and renal failure can increase toxicity.

Clinical Features

Tintinalli Source Check
SeverityTypical FeaturesDisposition Thinking
MildNausea, vomiting, fatigue, lethargy, fine tremorObservation/serial levels if acute; assess risk factors.
ModerateConfusion, agitation, dysarthria, ataxia, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, nystagmusAdmit; IV saline; serial levels.
SevereComa, seizures, myoclonus, hyperthermia, dysrhythmias, AV block, collapseICU; consider extracorporeal removal.

Diagnosis

Tintinalli Source Check
Serial lithium levelsEspecially important in acute/sustained-release ingestion.
Renal and sodium statusBMP, creatinine, sodium, urine concentrating ability when chronic toxicity suspected.
Tube pitfallAvoid lithium heparin collection tubes; false elevation can happen.
ECGLook for T-wave changes, QT prolongation, bradycardia, AV block.

Treatment

Tintinalli Source Check
Core move: airway/supportive care, ECG monitoring, IV normal saline to restore euvolemia and renal elimination, serial levels. Activated charcoal is not useful.

Dialysis / Extracorporeal Removal

Lithium is dialyzable, but rebound can occur because lithium redistributes from intracellular/extravascular spaces back into serum after intermittent hemodialysis. Monitor levels after dialysis and repeat if needed.

Consider dialysisSevere toxicity, coma, seizure, life-threatening dysrhythmia, renal failure, rising/high levels.
Acute vs chronicChronic toxicity may need dialysis at lower levels because CNS burden is higher.
ReboundRecheck levels after dialysis; repeat treatment if levels rise or symptoms recur.

Drug Dose Reference

InterventionReferenceBoard Caution
IV normal salineBolus 20 mL/kg if volume depleted, then 1.5-2x maintenance as toleratedGoal is euvolemia and renal lithium elimination; avoid volume overload.
Whole-bowel irrigationPEG solution around 2 L/h in adults when awake/airway protectedOnly selected sustained-release ingestion; contraindicated if obstruction/ileus/unstable airway.
Activated charcoalNot useful for lithiumDo not pick charcoal as the key answer for isolated lithium.
SeizuresIV benzodiazepinesSupport airway and consider dialysis for severe toxicity.
HemodialysisConsult nephrology/toxicology early for severe toxicity or high-risk levelsMonitor for rebound and repeat if needed.

Disposition

Tintinalli Source Check
Disposition: sustained-release acute ingestion gets admitted regardless of initial level. Moderate toxicity admits. Severe toxicity goes ICU with dialysis consideration.

Key Points

Charcoal does not bind lithiumDo not choose activated charcoal as isolated lithium therapy.
Acute vs chronicChronic toxicity is neurologic and can be severe at lower serum levels.
Serial levelsOne level is not enough after acute/sustained-release ingestion.
Normal salineRestore volume and sodium to promote renal elimination.
Interaction listNSAIDs, diuretics, ACEi/ARB, dehydration, renal failure.
DialysisSevere symptoms, renal failure, high/rising levels; watch rebound.
Tube pitfallDo not use lithium heparin tubes.
Sustained-releaseAdmit even if initial level is low.

Chapter Assessment

Which pattern is most concerning for chronic lithium toxicity?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. GI symptoms only after a single acute ingestion
Incorrect choice
Acute toxicity often starts GI-predominant; chronic toxicity is more neurologic.
B. Confusion, coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria in a chronic user
Correct choice
Neurologic findings predominate in chronic toxicity and correlate poorly with serum levels.
C. Miosis and respiratory depression
Incorrect choice
This is opioid-like.
D. Dry skin and absent bowel sounds only
Incorrect choice
This is anticholinergic-like.

Lithium serum level is best described as:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Always perfectly predicts clinical severity
Incorrect choice
Clinical symptoms often matter more than the level.
B. A marker of exposure but poor predictor of severity, especially chronic toxicity
Correct choice
Tintinalli emphasizes serum concentrations can mark exposure but poorly predict severity.
C. Never useful
Incorrect choice
Serial levels are still important for monitoring.
D. Only useful if drawn in a lithium heparin tube
Incorrect choice
Lithium heparin tubes can falsely elevate results and should be avoided.

Which GI decontamination strategy has a role in selected sustained-release lithium ingestion?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Activated charcoal
Incorrect choice
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium well.
B. Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
Correct choice
Whole-bowel irrigation is the only GI decontamination with a role for awake sustained-release ingestions.
C. Ipecac
Incorrect choice
Ipecac is not recommended.
D. Urinary acidification
Incorrect choice
Not GI decontamination and not useful.

Initial fluid therapy for lithium toxicity generally aims to:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Restrict all fluids
Incorrect choice
Volume depletion worsens lithium retention.
B. Restore euvolemia and normal renal elimination with IV normal saline
Correct choice
Normal saline restores renal perfusion and sodium/volume status.
C. Force diuresis with loop/thiazide diuretics
Incorrect choice
Loop/thiazide diuretics can promote water loss and worsen lithium concentration.
D. Give hypotonic free water only
Incorrect choice
Not the usual strategy and risks hyponatremia.

Which medication class can increase lithium toxicity by affecting renal sodium/water handling?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. NSAIDs
Correct choice
NSAIDs, diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs are classic lithium interaction risks.
B. Inhaled albuterol
Incorrect choice
Not a classic lithium-retention drug.
C. Acetaminophen
Incorrect choice
Generally not the key interaction.
D. Topical lidocaine
Incorrect choice
Not relevant.

Seizures in severe lithium toxicity should be treated with:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. IV benzodiazepines
Correct choice
Tintinalli lists IV benzodiazepines for seizures in severe toxicity.
B. Physostigmine
Incorrect choice
Not indicated.
C. Naloxone
Incorrect choice
Opioid antidote.
D. Sodium nitrite
Incorrect choice
Cyanide antidote kit component.

A patient with acute sustained-release lithium ingestion should be:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Discharged if first level is low
Incorrect choice
Delayed absorption makes the first level misleading.
B. Admitted regardless of initial lithium level and observed for toxicity
Correct choice
Tintinalli recommends admission regardless of serum level for acute sustained-release ingestion.
C. Given activated charcoal and discharged
Incorrect choice
Charcoal does not bind lithium well.
D. Observed for 30 minutes only
Incorrect choice
Far too short.

Extracorporeal removal/hemodialysis should be considered especially for:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Severe toxicity or renal failure/inability to tolerate fluids with high/rising levels
Correct choice
Dialysis is used for severe toxicity and selected high-level/renal-failure cases.
B. Any mild nausea with level 0.8
Incorrect choice
Mild therapeutic range symptoms are not an indication.
C. All patients taking lithium therapeutically
Incorrect choice
No.
D. Only if activated charcoal fails
Incorrect choice
Charcoal is not useful, so this framing is wrong.

Which lab collection pitfall matters in lithium toxicity?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Lithium heparin tubes can falsely elevate lithium levels
Correct choice
Tintinalli warns lithium heparin tubes may cause falsely positive/elevated lithium results.
B. Serum sodium always falsely low
Incorrect choice
No.
C. Troponin cannot be measured
Incorrect choice
No.
D. CBC invalidates lithium level
Incorrect choice
No.

Disposition for moderate lithium toxicity is:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Discharge after one normal vital sign set
Incorrect choice
Unsafe.
B. Admission; severe toxicity needs ICU and dialysis consideration
Correct choice
Moderate toxicity requires admission; severe toxicity requires ICU/extracorporeal consideration.
C. No serial levels needed
Incorrect choice
Serial levels are part of management.
D. Psychiatric clearance only
Incorrect choice
Medical toxicity must be handled first.
